newsitem.title: UK: Euro products outlook - gas oil to support margins.
newsitem.headline: Euro products outlook - gas oil to support margins.

text.p: European oil products are likely to remain relatively stable this week with steady interest for gas oil providing some support for refiners' margins, traders and brokers said.
A combination of steady heating oil demand and a dearth of refinery grade gas oil is likely to keep prices steady to firmer.
Premiums to the February IPE futures contract could trade unchanged in a range around +$8/10 for prompt material, with end-month deals around $2 less.
"Once you get around to offering +$11/12 over February you could cover from the barge market and then freight it," a trader said.

Traders saw the likely emergence of a two-tier low sulphur diesel market, split between small parcels into Bordeaux and large Algerian cargoes that will be difficult to place other than in the ARA barge market.

In barges, confusion over deliveries caused by ice in the ARA waterways will firm the outright price by raising demurrage and freight costs, traders said. If the weather continues at Friday's levels premiums are likely to remain unchanged at around Feb +$6/7 but could spike if the mercury descends further to Arctic levels.
European gasoline will continue to feel the draw from the U.S despite last week's NYMEX losses and the high cost of spot freight rates, traders said.
"Local demand is not up to much so I wouldn't be surprised to see European prices dipping to keep in line with the U.S," said one dealer.
Up to one million tonnes is loading in January and shipping brokers say there is still interest in finding tankers.
U.S interest for naphtha will remain this week although working cargoes transatlantic is expected to become increasingly difficult, but much depends on when freight costs were fixed.

"If a company has ships, the costs could be put on the shipping arm," said one trader. Light virgin material has been thinned following deals last week at $4 above quotes but if any deals are concluded this week they should be below this level, said one dealer.
High and low sulphur fuel oil are unlikely to make much upwards progress this week after last week's tumble.

The falls were rooted in a lacklustre demand outlook for January - with forecasts that Italy, the world's largest buyer of low sulphur fuel oil, is unlikely to step into the market to buy large quantities soon.

High sulphur fuel oil also appears to have taken a knock and with forecasts for warmer weather, dealers see no reason for it to return to its earlier higher levels. Utility spot demand for the rest of the month is not thought to be very strong. But in the Mediterranean, good demand for bunkers is likely to provide some support, and fresh Romanian demand has taken out some of January's length.
